A1.justification: Both PDFs present CTSketch. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial rearrangement of supporting material.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original CTSketch benchmark accuracies, learning curves, computational timings, and sketching-rank experiments.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices C–D report original CTSketch evaluations, including retained benchmarks and new decomposition and sketching-method ablations.

M1.justification: Program decomposition, tensor initialization and sketching, contraction-based training, RBF/one-hot alternatives, and symbolic testing remain unchanged. The bounded-loop example and expanded contraction equations clarify the existing procedure. Alternative sketching methods are tested within its already stated interchangeable design.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same MNIST sum and multi-digit addition sizes, visual Sudoku, Sudoku solving, HWF, leaf identification, and scene classification. The new ablations reuse sum16, sum4, and HWF. The sum4 and add1 results omitted from v2's main summary remain in its appendix.

E2.justification: The main neurosymbolic comparator set is retained. New comparisons introduce FULL and FULL+RBF controls on sum16 and CP, Tucker, and Tensor Ring alternatives to Tensor Train in Tables 6–7. IndeCateR also joins the add100 timing comparison, which previously plotted only CTSketch.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported sum1024 training set from 5K to 4K examples. Appendix C.1 changes IndeCateR's add100 budget from 15 to 45 epochs. New ablations vary decomposition depth, tensor representation, and sketching method/rank, measuring storage and training time alongside accuracy. The revised descriptions do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained HWF rank-sensitivity study, Appendix D adds substantial tests of the central design choices. Table 6 separates program decomposition, sketching, and RBF effects on sum16; Table 7 compares sketching families on sum4 and HWF. These provide new evidence about component contributions and accuracy, memory, and runtime tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten random seeds and report standard deviations. Uncertainty omitted from v2's compact main table remains in Appendix C's full tables. Calling these one-sigma standard deviations and extending the same reporting format to additional results does not change the statistical practice.

E6.justification: Most retained benchmark scores are unchanged, but v2 replaces DSL's sum64 timeout with 0.78 ± 0.32% and IndeCateR's add100 error with 6.4 ± 6.6%; the latter accompanies a changed training budget. Tables 6–7 add substantial new result sets on decomposition and sketching alternatives, including memory/runtime tradeoffs and CP's weaker HWF performance. The add100 learning curves are also updated.

T1.justification: The central Theorem 3.2 changes its bound from sqrt(2)||p||_F e to sqrt(2)||p||_F sqrt(floor(4e^2)), where e is the tensor reconstruction error. Appendix B replaces the original final proof step with a mismatch-count argument using a 0.5 error threshold. This substantively revises the guarantee and its reasoning.

C1.justification: The main contributions and scalability claims remain. However, v2's abstract explicitly attributes high accuracy on thousand-input tasks to the neural predictors, and its conclusion removes the broader high-accuracy wording. This narrows the claim consistently with the retained 2.73% sum1024 task accuracy and 93.69% per-digit accuracy.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly discusses why decomposition alone can encounter memory limits, attributes slower deeper sketched computations to repeated RBF transformations, and attributes CP's weak HWF performance to its rank-one structure. It also explains the choice of Tensor Train through storage efficiency despite alternatives' slightly higher accuracy. The principal manual-decomposition limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly discloses the learning-rate search grid and reuse of models, prompts, and configurations for GPT-based tasks. Table 5 identifies borrowed DSL and A-NeSI results. Appendix E adds implementation provenance, TensorLy and CLIP usage, and software/dataset licenses. Existing hardware, CTSketch hyperparameters, and code access are retained.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning through arithmetic/probabilistic circuits, PyJuice, KLay, PLIAt, and TerpreT. It contrasts GPU execution, integer-arithmetic restrictions, and program induction with CTSketch's approach. Additional sketching and software references support the new experiments and disclosures.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanations receive selective rewrites, including explicit contraction forms and a bounded-loop example. Pseudocode moves to Appendix A, supporting sections are reorganized, and citation style and author/funding text change. The main seven-section narrative remains substantially intact.

P2.justification: The presentation is substantially reorganized: v2 merges arithmetic results into a compact main table, relocates complete uncertainty-bearing tables, combines the traditional-benchmark subtables, and adds two ablation tables. The add100 plot is relocated and revised with another comparator and a shorter time axis; other plots are resized or rearranged. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: Tables 6–7 strengthen evidence about the method's components and memory/accuracy tradeoffs, while the narrower large-input accuracy claim better matches the retained results. Revised proof reasoning, implementation disclosures, and research positioning improve assessability. These are meaningful but bounded gains: the theoretical bound still concerns reconstructed tensors rather than the implemented RBF-based inference.
